Question ten. What is a quasi-experiment, and how does difference-in-differences work? Sometimes you can't randomize: a policy starts in one city and not in another. A quasi-experiment makes use of that natural split. In this simulation, the treated city's weekly sign-ups rose eight point nine after the policy. The comparison city rose two point four over the same weeks, with no policy at all. The difference of those differences, D I D for short, is six point five, close to the true effect of six. It rests on parallel trends: without the policy, the two lines would have kept moving together.

Four left. Each one is a definition and a reason. The average treatment effect, A T E, is averaged over everyone. The average treatment effect on the treated, A T T, only over those who actually got it. A randomized test makes them match. Observational data can pull them apart. Long-running experiments drift: seasons turn, and other launches land on the same users. Freeze the scope, run at least one full business cycle, and set the end date in advance. A holdback keeps a few percent of users on the old version after launch, to check months later that the win lasted. And a meta-analysis pools many experiments, weighting each by its precision rather than averaging headlines. Watch for the winner's curse: at twenty percent power, the results that reached significance overstate the true effect more than twofold. Every answer here assumed someone had already chosen what to test and what to count. Making that choice is the product-sense round. Next: product sense and metrics.
